hints: Relate the tangent gradient to the geometry of the normal triangle $PMN$.
The normal has gradient $-dx/dy$; its rise from $N$ to $P$ is $y$ and its horizontal run has magnitude $MN$.
Equating these signed or magnitude gradients gives the required ratio, with the diagram fixing the positive lengths.
walkthrough: Let $m = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$ be the gradient of the tangent to the curve at $P(x, y)$.
Since the normal at $P$ is perpendicular to the tangent, the gradient of the normal is $m_{\text{normal}} = -\dfrac{1}{m} = -\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{d}y/\mathrm{d}x}$.

From the geometry of the right-angled triangle $PMN$, where $M$ has coordinates $(x, 0)$ and $P$ has coordinates $(x, y)$, the vertical leg is $PM = y$.
The horizontal displacement from $N$ to $M$ along the $x$-axis is $MN = x_N - x_M$, so the slope of line segment $PN$ is $-\dfrac{PM}{MN} = -\dfrac{y}{MN}$.

Equate the two expressions for the slope of the normal:
$$-\dfrac{y}{MN} = -\dfrac{1}{\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}}$$
$$\dfrac{y}{MN} = \dfrac{1}{\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}} \implies \dfrac{MN}{y} = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$$
This completes the proof.

hints: Use the triangle-area formula together with the ratio proved in part (i).
Equate this area to $\tan x$ and simplify to the stated differential equation.
walkthrough:
Write the formula for the area of the right-angled triangle $PMN$ with base $MN$ and height $PM = y$:
$$\text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} = \dfrac{1}{2}(MN)(y)$$

From part (a)(i), express $MN$ in terms of $y$ and $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$:
$$MN = y\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$$

Substitute this into the area formula:
$$\text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(y\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}\right)(y) = \dfrac{1}{2}y^2\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$$

Equate the area expression to the given value $\tan x$:
$$\dfrac{1}{2}y^2\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \tan x$$
This completes the proof.

hints: Separate the differential equation and integrate both sides before applying the initial condition.
From $\frac12y^2dy/dx=\tan x$, integrate $\frac12y^2dy=\tan x\,dx$ to obtain a cubic term and $-\ln(\cos x)$.
Use $y=1$ at $x=0$ to determine the constant.
Isolate $y^3$ and take the real cube root, noting $0\le x<\pi/2$.
walkthrough:
Separate variables in the differential equation $\dfrac{1}{2}y^2\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \tan x$:
$$\dfrac{1}{2}y^2\,\mathrm{d}y = \tan x\,\mathrm{d}x$$

Integrate both sides:
$$\int \dfrac{1}{2}y^2\,\mathrm{d}y = \int \tan x\,\mathrm{d}x$$
$$\dfrac{1}{6}y^3 = -\ln(\cos x) + c$$

Use the initial condition $y = 1$ when $x = 0$ to determine $c$:
$$\dfrac{1}{6}(1)^3 = -\ln(\cos 0) + c$$
$$\dfrac{1}{6} = -\ln(1) + c$$
$$\dfrac{1}{6} = 0 + c \implies c = \dfrac{1}{6}$$

Multiply through by $6$ to isolate $y^3$:
$$y^3 = 1 - 6\ln(\cos x)$$

Take the cube root to express $y$ explicitly in terms of $x$:
$$y = \left(1 - 6\ln(\cos x)\right)^{\frac{1}{3}} = \sqrt[3]{1 - 6\ln(\cos x)}$$
